clue.text: British truth-twisters abandoning left for certain Bushes

indicators.note: abandoning tells us a letter is left behind, so it drops out of the word for truth-twisters

parts.note: people who twist the truth are liars

explanation.surface: British fibbers ditch the left wing for a certain famous political family called Bush.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bushes' with its capital letter points to the American presidents, but it is a plain plural of bush here.
explanation.definitionFit: Briars are thorny wild shrubs such as the wild rose, so they are particular kinds of bush.

clue.text: Monk possibly gets leader of rebels in trouble

indicators.note: in places the first letter of rebels inside the word for trouble

parts.note: bother is trouble or fuss

indicators.note: leader of means the first letter

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A monk gets into difficulty with the ringleader of a rebellion.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of a monastic order are addressed as Brother, so a monk is one example.

clue.text: Bits of Shakespeare sonnets, or their subtext?

parts.note: read as three short words, a confession of bisexuality that some find beneath sonnets addressed to both a young man and a dark lady

explanation.surface: Parts of the Sonnets, or the message hiding beneath them?
explanation.walkthrough: The sonnets are addressed to both a young man and a woman, hence the joking reading I AM BI (bisexual).
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's sonnets are in iambic pentameter, so their metrical units are iambs, plural here in the Latin form.

clue.text: Criticises puzzles, getting wrong end of stick

indicators.note: getting wrong means a letter from the start of stick is swapped for the one at the other end

parts.note: rebuses are picture puzzles

indicators.note: end of means the last letter of stick

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone attacks puzzles after misunderstanding them.
explanation.walkthrough: Stick runs from S to K; in REBUSES the second S, stick's first letter, is replaced with K, its other end.
explanation.definitionFit: To rebuke is to reprimand or scold, which is to criticise sharply.

clue.text: Old man and wife doubled up for something seedy

indicators.note: doubled up says the old man and wife pair is written a second time straight after the first

parts.note: an old man is a father, informally PA

explanation.surface: An elderly couple doubled over might suggest something shady going on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'doubled up' tells you to write the father-and-wife pair twice over.
explanation.definitionFit: The pawpaw, another name for papaya, is a tropical fruit full of black seeds; 'seedy' usually means shabby.

clue.text: Film director's short with Romeo who should know his lines

indicators.note: short means his name loses its last letter

parts.note: Ang Lee is the Taiwanese-born film director
R is Romeo in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A director is curt with the actor playing Romeo, who ought to have learnt his script.
explanation.walkthrough: 'who should know his lines' suggests an actor beside Romeo; the lines are fishing lines.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who fishes with rod and line needs to know about fishing tackle, a pun on actors' lines.

clue.text: As part of quiet time, cheeky chappies hide from nanny, maybe

indicators.note: As part of means the cheeky chappies sit inside the quiet and time letters

parts.note: P is piano, the musical abbreviation for quiet
arch means playfully mischievous, cheeky
chappies are men

explanation.surface: During a quiet spell, two cheeky lads hide from their nanny.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hide from nanny' looks like children dodging a carer; it means skin from a nanny goat, and 'hide' is a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Parchment is writing material made from animal skin, such as that of a goat, so goatskin may become parchment.

clue.text: See 26
Clever saint and I agree to feed five thousand — there'll be no fish in it, though

definitions.text: there'll be no fish in it, though

indicators.note: to feed means the rearranged letters go into the Roman numerals, like food into a mouth

parts.note: V is the Roman numeral for five
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand

indicators.note: clever is read as cleverly worked, so the letters that follow are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Echoes the miracle of feeding the five thousand with loaves and fishes, minus the fish.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Gospels Jesus fed five thousand people with loaves and fishes; here the five thousand become Roman numerals, and the feast has no fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Vegetarianism is a diet without meat or fish, so this is a meal plan with no fish in it.

clue.text: Stray from the city all roads lead back to (they say)

indicators.note: they say marks a word that is spoken, so the city's name stands for a word sounding the same

parts.words: the city all roads lead back to
parts.note: the proverb says all roads lead to Rome

explanation.surface: Someone wanders off from the city that every road supposedly returns to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'they say' looks like it just hedges the proverb, but it is the sound signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To stray is to wander without a fixed course, which is exactly what roaming is.

clue.text: Cosy area behind pub that keeps a lot of green around

definitions.text: Cosy area behind pub that keeps a lot of green around

indicators.note: behind means the cosy area comes after the pub in the answer
that keeps means the pub word holds another piece inside it

parts.note: a bar is a pub

indicators.note: around signals that the shortened green word is turned round and read backwards
a lot of means most but not all, so the last letter of green goes

parts.note: taken as written
a den is a snug, cosy room

explanation.surface: A snug spot at the back of a pub, surrounded by greenery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a lot of' is a trimming signal: most of the word, not all. The whole clue also describes the answer, so it is read twice.
explanation.definitionFit: A pub's garden is an outdoor seating space, usually planted and leafy, at the back of the premises.

clue.text: Scream when ogre traps recurring character in his wicked lair

indicators.note: traps means the ogre's name closes round another letter, holding it inside

parts.note: Shrek is the ogre of the animated films

parts.words: recurring character in his wicked lair
parts.note: the letter I recurs through 'his wicked lair', appearing three times

explanation.surface: A cry rings out as a monster holds someone captive in his evil den.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recurring character' is not a person who keeps appearing in a story but a letter that repeats in the next few words.
explanation.definitionFit: A shriek is a high piercing cry, a close synonym of a scream.

clue.text: Like youth with mouth, it must be seen and not heard

definitions.text: Like youth with mouth, it must be seen and not heard

parts.words: Like youth with mouth, it must be seen and not heard
parts.note: youth and mouth look as if they rhyme on the page but do not when spoken; the proverb about children is twisted

explanation.walkthrough: The clue borrows 'children should be seen and not heard'; the pair youth and mouth match only to the eye.
explanation.definitionFit: This term names a pair of words spelt alike at the end but pronounced differently, a rhyme for the eye only.

clue.text: Sports star may get this £1000 bit of activewear in three sizes

parts.note: a grand is slang for a thousand pounds

indicators.note: in places the activewear letter inside the run of size letters

parts.note: S, L and M are clothing sizes small, large and medium

indicators.note: bit of means just the first letter of activewear is used

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An athlete might be handed an expensive sports top available in three sizes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sports star may get this' sounds like a reward of kit; it is the definition, a top tennis or golf achievement.
explanation.definitionFit: Winning all of a sport's major tournaments in one season is the crowning feat a top player may achieve.

clue.text: Needing content for feature, paps went back daily?

indicators.note: back means the hidden letters are read from right to left
content for means the answer lies within the following words

parts.note: taken as written; 'went' joins the hidden stretch

explanation.surface: Paparazzi retreated after getting material for a magazine feature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'went back' reads like the photographers retreating; 'went' is part of the hiding place and 'back' is the reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A daily is a paper published every day, so a newspaper is an example of one, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Swiss capital invested in cybernetics

indicators.note: invested in means the city's name is tucked inside the following word

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Switzerland's money has been put into robotics research.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swiss capital' looks like money (francs) going into an investment, but it is the city.
explanation.definitionFit: Bern is the seat of the Swiss federal government and the country's de facto capital city.

clue.text: Throw about to get wicket?

indicators.note: to get means the reversed word takes another letter inside it
about means the throw word is turned round

parts.note: to lob is to throw high
W is the cricket scoring abbreviation for a wicket

explanation.surface: A cricketer hurls the ball, hoping to take a wicket.
explanation.walkthrough: BOL (LOB backwards) takes W inside. In cricket the bowler delivers the ball to the batter, hoping to hit the wicket.
explanation.definitionFit: Delivering the ball overarm to the batsman in cricket is a throw of sorts aimed at taking a wicket.

clue.text: Shops expect increase in salary to be announced

indicators.note: to be announced means the words are spoken, so the spelling follows what is heard

parts.note: I bet means I expect, and a raise is a rise in salary

explanation.surface: Retail stores anticipate a pay rise being declared.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shops' looks like a noun for stores; it is a verb meaning informs on someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To shop someone is British slang for informing on them to the police, a kind of treachery.

clue.text: Sorcerer ultimately in two minds about tempest

indicators.note: in places the sorcerer's final letter inside the rearranged letters
about here means moved around, so the letters of two minds are shuffled

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: ultimately means only the last letter of sorcerer is used

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A magician unsure what to do about a storm, as in Prospero in The Tempest.
explanation.walkthrough: TWO MINDS rearranged gives WINDSTOM, and R (the end of Sorcerer) sits in it.
explanation.definitionFit: A tempest is a violent storm with high winds, which is what this compound word describes.

clue.text: A run of notes getting higher or lower

parts.note: the run of notes begins on the note D
the next note in the run is E flat, a semitone above D
the run ends on E, a semitone above the E flat before it, so the notes keep climbing

explanation.surface: A musical scale that climbs or descends.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole phrase 'A run of notes getting higher' describes D, E flat, E, each a semitone higher; the pieces are split only to show where each note comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: To deflate something is to let air out, bringing it down or lowering it, including someone's mood.

clue.text: Comic librettist weirdly wants the Three Tenors

indicators.note: weirdly means the letters of librettist are rearranged once the tenors are taken out

parts.note: taken as written
T is the abbreviation for tenor in choral parts, so three tenors are TTT

explanation.surface: An absurd opera lyricist demands the famous trio of singers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wants' means lacks: remove three Ts from LIBRETTIST and rearrange what is left. The Three Tenors were Pavarotti, Domingo and Carreras.
explanation.definitionFit: Something risible provokes laughter, which is what a comic thing is.

clue.text: Party leaders to mess around in field

parts.note: a do is a party

indicators.note: leaders means the opening letters of the next two words

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Political party chiefs fool about out in a meadow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party leaders' reads as one phrase, but the party is DO and 'leaders' works on the words after.
explanation.definitionFit: A domain is an area of knowledge or responsibility, just as a field is one's sphere of expertise.

clue.text: Leave domesticated animals to fly west with swallow

indicators.note: in an across answer, flying west means going right to left, so the word is turned round

parts.note: pets are domesticated animals
to down a drink is to swallow it

explanation.surface: Household pets head west, along with a migrating swallow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swallow' looks like the bird, keeping company with the flying animals, but it is a verb meaning to gulp.
explanation.definitionFit: To leave a post such as a job or office is to resign from it, which this phrase means.

clue.text: On easy street, being as liberated as possible

parts.note: free and easy go together: relaxed, unconstrained

explanation.surface: Someone comfortably off, on Easy Street, enjoys the utmost liberty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On easy street' is an idiom for being well off; here it splits into pieces, with 'On' showing the street comes after.
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of free means having the greatest liberty, the least constraint of anyone.

clue.text: Pop to Methuselah's place, finally, and see if he's in for callers?

indicators.note: finally means only the last letter of place

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: for callers means the word is heard, as by someone calling at the door

parts.note: to knock on a door is to check whether someone is in

explanation.surface: A visitor drops in at old Methuselah's house and raps to see if he is home.
explanation.walkthrough: Methuselah is the setter's pseudonym. In Genesis Enoch is Methuselah's father, so 'Pop' means dad.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Bible Enoch fathered Methuselah, so he is Methuselah's dad, his pop.

clue.text: Travelling space, NASA orbits source of ice water

indicators.note: orbits means the rearranged letters circle round another, holding it inside
travelling suggests movement, so the letters of space and NASA are moved about

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: source of means the first letter of ice

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A NASA craft circles in space around a source of ice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Travelling' and 'orbits' both sound like spaceflight, but one shuffles letters and the other wraps them round a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The Caspian Sea is the world's largest inland body of water, between Europe and Asia.

clue.text: Spheres or a load of balls

parts.note: taken as written
a load of balls is British slang for nonsense, as is BS, short for bullshit

explanation.surface: Round objects, or just a pile of balls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a load of balls' looks like a heap of spheres, echoing the definition, but it is slang for nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: An orb is a globe or ball shape, so orbs are spheres.

clue.text: Perhaps I win as manager (or was I a German in tears?)

indicators.note: tears here means rips apart, so the letters of the phrase are torn up and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A football boss hopes to win, then wonders tearfully whether people took her for German.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tears' looks like crying; it means ripping. The bracketed words also hint that 'I win as manager' is an anagram too.
explanation.definitionFit: Sarina Wiegman, a Dutch coach, managed England's women to Euro 2022 victory, so she could say she won as manager.

clue.text: One nerdy follower of Phi cracks themes on a regular basis

indicators.note: cracks means the Greek letter breaks into the middle of the other piece
on a regular basis means every other letter of themes is taken

parts.note: taken as written
chi follows phi in the Greek alphabet; Phi is also a regular Independent setter

explanation.surface: A nerdy fan of the setter Phi solves themed puzzles regularly.
explanation.walkthrough: Phi is the setter who usually has the Friday slot in the Independent; here the name is the Greek letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A techie is a person keen on technology, often seen as a geek or a nerd.
